flashcards.q: Why does accessing memory on a remote NUMA node cost more than accessing local memory, and by roughly how much?
flashcards.a: Each CPU socket has its own locally-attached memory controller; remote access crosses an inter-socket interconnect (QPI/UPI, Infinity Fabric), commonly cited around 1.5-2x local DRAM latency or more. Fix: numactl --cpunodebind/--membind to keep threads and memory on the same node, or kernel NUMA balancing.

flashcards.q: Why do production runbooks for Redis/MongoDB commonly say to disable Transparent Huge Pages (THP)?
flashcards.a: THP's background page-promotion/compaction work can happen synchronously on the allocation path, and for workloads with frequent small allocations plus fork()-based background saves (Redis/MongoDB's pattern), that compaction stall causes multi-ms to multi-hundred-ms latency spikes — the opposite of THP's intended TLB-miss-reduction benefit for this specific allocation pattern.

flashcards.q: What two Linux kernel primitives actually implement container isolation, and how does this differ from VM isolation?
flashcards.a: Namespaces (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user) give a process group its own view of kernel resources; cgroups enforce resource limits. Every container still runs on the SAME host kernel — no hypervisor-enforced hardware boundary — so a kernel escape compromises the whole host, unlike a VM escape which must break a much narrower hypervisor boundary.

flashcards.q: What mechanisms provide real hardware-backed isolation for genuinely untrusted multi-tenant workloads beyond plain containers?
flashcards.a: gVisor (a userspace kernel intercepting syscalls to shrink host kernel attack surface) or Firecracker/Kata Containers (lightweight VMs giving genuine hypervisor isolation at near-container startup speed) — used specifically because namespace/cgroup isolation alone is judged insufficient for adversarial multi-tenancy.
